As the primaries proceeded, they were overshadowed by the ___E:COVID-19 pandemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic)___ , which was declared to be a global pandemic on March 11, 2020. On April 8, 2020, Biden became the presumptive Democratic nominee after Sanders (the only other candidate remaining) withdrew from the race.  In early June, Biden passed the threshold of 1,991 delegates to win the nomination.
Seven candidates received pledged delegates: Biden, Sanders, Warren, Bloomberg, Buttigieg, Senator ___E:Amy Klobuchar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Klobuchar)___ and U.S.

Biden and Harris won the presidency and vice presidency in the general election on November 3, defeating the Republican ticket of President ___E:Donald Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)___ and Vice President ___E:Mike Pence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence)___ .

After ___E:Hillary Clinton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton)___ 's loss in the ___E:previous election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election)___ , many felt the Democratic Party lacked a clear leading figure.

Divisions remained in the party following the ___E:2016 primaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries)___ , which pitted Clinton against ___E:Bernie Sanders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders)___ .

Between the 2016 election and the ___E:2018 midterm elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_midterm_elections)___ , Senate Democrats generally shifted to the ___E:political left U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_liberalism_in_the_United_States)___ in relation to college tuition, healthcare, and immigration.

The ___E:2018 elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_elections)___ saw the Democratic Party regain the House of Representatives for the first time in eight years, picking up seats in both urban and suburban districts.

On August 25, 2018, the ___E:Democratic National Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee)___ (DNC) members passed reforms to the Democratic Party's primary process in order to increase participation  and ensure transparency.

State parties are encouraged to use a government-run primary whenever available and increase the accessibility of their primary through ___E:same-day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-day_voter_registration)___ or ___E:automatic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_voter_registration)___ registration and same-day party switching.
Caucuses are required to have absentee voting, or to otherwise allow those who cannot participate in person to be included.

Independent of the results of the primaries and caucuses, the Democratic Party, from its group of party leaders and elected officials, also appointed 771 [a] unpledged delegates ( ___E:superdelegates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_automatic_delegates_at_the_2020_Democratic_National_Convention)___ ) to participate in its national convention.

In contrast to all previous election cycles since superdelegates were introduced in 1984, superdelegates will no longer have the right to cast decisive votes on the convention's first ballot for the presidential nomination.

They will be allowed to cast non-decisive votes if a candidate has clinched the nomination before the first ballot, or decisive votes on subsequent ballots in a ___E:contested convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brokered_convention)___ .
In that case, the number of votes required shall increase to a majority of pledged and superdelegates combined.
Superdelegates are not precluded from publicly endorsing a candidate before the convention.
There were a number of changes to the process of nomination at the state level.

A decline in the number of caucuses occurred after 2016. Democrats in Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Kansas, Maine, Minnesota, Nebraska, North Dakota, and Washington all switched from various forms of caucuses to primaries.
Hawaii, Kansas, and North Dakota switched to party-run " ___E:firehouse primaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firehouse_primary)___ ".
This resulted in the lowest number of caucuses in the Democratic Party's recent history.
Only three states (Iowa, Nevada, and Wyoming) and four territories (American Samoa, Guam, Northern Marianas, and U.S.

Virgin Islands) used them. Six states were approved in 2019 by the DNC to use ___E:ranked-choice voting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranked-choice_voting_in_the_United_States)___ in the primaries: Alaska, Hawaii, Kansas, and Wyoming for all voters; Iowa and Nevada for absentee voters.

Rather than eliminating candidates until a single winner is chosen, voters' choices were reallocated until all remaining candidates have at least 15%, the threshold to receive delegates to the convention.

Several states which did not use paper ballots widely in 2016 and 2018, ___E:adopted U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_audit#Current_practices_in_election_results_auditing_in_the_United_States)___ them for the 2020 primary and general elections,  to minimize potential interference in vote tallies, a concern raised by intelligence officials,  election officials  and the public.

The move to paper ballots enabled audits to start where they had not been possible before, and in 2020 about half the states ___E:audit samples U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_audit#Overview)___ of primary ballots to measure accuracy of the reported results.

Audits of caucus results depend on party rules, and the ___E:Iowa Democratic party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Iowa_Democratic_caucuses#Inconsistencies_in_votes)___ investigated inaccuracies in precinct reports, resolved enough to be sure the delegate allocations were correct, and decided it did not have authority or time to correct all errors.

The number of pledged delegates from each state is proportional to the state's share of the ___E:electoral college U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_electoral_college)___ , and to the state's past Democratic votes for president.
Thus less weight is given to swing states and Republican states, while more weight is given to strongly Democratic states, in choosing a nominee.
Six pledged delegates are assigned to each territory, 44 to Puerto Rico, and 12 to Democrats Abroad.
Each jurisdiction can also earn bonus delegates by holding primaries after March or in clusters of 3 or more neighboring states.

Within states, a quarter of pledged delegates are allocated to candidates based on statewide vote totals, and the rest typically based on votes in each congressional district, although some states use divisions other than congressional districts.
For example, Texas uses ___E:state Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Senate)___ districts.
Districts which have voted Democratic in the past get more delegates, and fewer delegates are allocated for swing districts and Republican districts.

For example, House Speaker Pelosi's strongly Democratic ___E:district 12 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California%27s_12th_congressional_district)___ has 7 delegates, or one per 109,000 people, and a swing district, ___E:CA-10 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California%27s_10th_congressional_district)___ , which became Democratic in 2018, has 4 delegates, or one per 190,000 people.

Candidates who received under 15% of the votes in a state or district didn't get any delegates from that area. Candidates who got 15% or more of the votes divided delegates in proportion to their votes.
These rules apply at the state level to state delegates and within each district for those delegates.
The 15% threshold was established in 1992  to limit "fringe" candidates.

The threshold now means that any sector of the party (moderate, progressive, etc.) which produces many candidates, thus dividing supporters' votes, may win few delegates, even if it wins a majority of votes.
